nameStory: The Common Pandora gets its name from the mythical Pandora's box, though unlike that tale of unleashed troubles, this little clam keeps its secrets safely tucked inside its peculiar asymmetrical shell. The scientific name honors Augustus Addison Gould, a 19th-century Boston physician and naturalist who cataloged many New England mollusks.
description: The Common Pandora is a small, flattened clam with a distinctly lopsided appearance that makes it easy to recognize among beach finds. Its thin, translucent shell rarely exceeds an inch in length and has an unusual rectangular shape that's longer than it is tall. Unlike most clams, the two halves of its shell are noticeably different sizes and shapes, giving it a quirky, asymmetrical look. This delicate bivalve lives buried in sandy and muddy seafloors along our coast.

idTips.label: Asymmetrical shell halves
idTips.description: The right valve is much flatter and smaller than the left valve, creating a distinctly lopsided appearance when viewed from the side - like someone sat on half the shell

idTips.label: Rectangular outline
idTips.description: Shell is longer than it is tall with a boxy, rectangular shape rather than the typical oval clam form - feels thin and fragile like a fingernail

idTips.label: Pearly interior
idTips.description: Inside surface has a beautiful pearlescent sheen that shifts from white to pale pink and blue as you tilt it in the light

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically less than an inch long, fitting easily on a child's thumbnail - much smaller than most clams you'll find on the beach

idTips.label: Translucent shell
idTips.description: When fresh, the thin shell is semi-transparent, allowing you to see shadows and light through it when held up to the sun

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth to the touch with very fine growth lines, lacking the heavy ridges or bumps of many other clams

habitat: Common Pandoras live in sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 100 feet deep. You'll find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches after storms, particularly on Cape Cod and the islands, though they occur along the entire New England coast. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often live alongside other small clams and marine worms in the sediment.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, often still retaining their pearlescent interior shine and thin, translucent appearance.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding shells on beaches during low tides, especially after rough weather stirs up the seafloor.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently bring shells to shore - look for the distinctive rectangular, lopsided shape among other beach debris.
seasonality.winter: Shells become more weathered and chalky white, but the asymmetrical shape remains the key identifying feature even in worn specimens.

funFact: The Common Pandora can actually swim by rapidly clapping its mismatched shell halves together - an unusual ability among clams that helps it escape from predators or rebury itself when exposed on the seafloor.
confusionNotes: The asymmetrical shell makes this species nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England clam - if the two shell halves look obviously different sizes, you've found a Pandora. Remember: "Pandora's lopsided box" for the uneven shell halves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "common," these clams are actually not frequently encountered alive by beachcombers since they live buried in subtidal sediments. Most people only see their empty shells that wash ashore, leading to some confusion about whether they're actually common in our waters.
compareHints: The Common Pandora is the only Pandora species regularly found in New England waters, making it unique in our region. Compared to other small, thin-shelled clams like tellins or macomas, the Pandora's dramatically asymmetrical shell halves and rectangular outline make it unmistakable. While other clams may have slight differences between their shell halves, none show the extreme size and shape differences seen in Pandoras.
